summary.lead: Official summary (Congressional Research Service, Introduced in Senate):

blocks.text: This bill reauthorizes through FY2025 the programs and activities of the National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA). The bill also revises certain existing NASA programs and establishes new programs related to space exploration, research, and technology.

For example, the bill directs NASA to continue its efforts to support crewed lunar landings and Mars explorations, including through partnerships with the private sector (i.e., the Moon to Mars and Artemis programs).

The bill also requires NASA to maintain the capability for a continuous human presence in low-Earth orbit until and beyond the retirement of the International Space Station (ISS). NASA may solicit proposals for the development of a commercial space station in low-Earth orbit. When such a station is ready, NASA must initiate an orderly transition of operations from the ISS to the commercial station. NASA must also develop a de-orbit vehicle for the eventual retirement of the ISS. (Low-Earth orbit encompasses orbits at an altitude of 1,200 miles or less.)

In addition, NASA is authorized to develop an architecture for lunar communications and navigation, and must develop a strategy to implement a standardized lunar time to support operations and infrastructure on and around the moon.
NASA must also continue to conduct research relating to advanced air mobility, unmanned aircraft systems (i.e., drones), and hypersonic technologies.
Finally, the bill requires the Government Accountability Office to report on fire and emergency services at NASA launch and reentry facilities.

This bill extends NASA's existing programs and activities through fiscal year 2025, and it also changes some current programs and creates new ones focused on space exploration, research, and technology. It directs NASA to keep working toward crewed landings on the Moon and exploration of Mars, including through partnerships with private companies. These efforts fall under the Moon to Mars and Artemis programs.

The bill requires NASA to keep a continuous human presence in low-Earth orbit, meaning orbits at an altitude of 1,200 miles or less, until and beyond the retirement of the International Space Station (ISS). NASA may ask companies to propose a commercial space station in low-Earth orbit. Once that station is ready, NASA must begin an orderly move of operations from the ISS to it. NASA must also develop a de-orbit vehicle, a spacecraft that would bring the ISS down when it is eventually retired.
The bill also allows NASA to design a system for communications and navigation on the Moon. It requires NASA to develop a plan for a standard lunar time to support activities on and around the Moon.
In addition, NASA must keep researching advanced air mobility, unmanned aircraft systems (drones), and hypersonic technologies.
Finally, the Government Accountability Office must report on fire and emergency services at NASA's launch and reentry facilities.
